subject: economics
title: Minimum Wage and Discrimination
welcome_lead: Two policy hot spots: floors on pay and unequal treatment.
meta_desc: A-Level Labour Markets: minimum wage and discrimination.
final_note: Minimum wages help most workers but risk job loss where demand is elastic.

concepts.def: Wage estimated to cover basic needs.
Unequal pay or hiring not based on productivity.
How responsive employment is to wages.
Reduction in pay gaps after a wage floor.

walkthroughs.body_html: Above the competitive wage, a minimum wage causes unemployment if labour demand is elastic. In a monopsony, it can raise both wages and employment.
Pay gaps may reflect productivity differences (training, hours) or true discrimination. Discrimination is inefficient - it leaves talent unused - and is illegal under equality law.
Anti-discrimination law, pay-gap reporting and equal-pay audits aim to close gaps. Higher minimum wages can compress wages but may push low-skill jobs into automation.

mcqs.q: Minimum wage above equilibrium in a competitive market typically causes:
options: Labour shortage
Some unemployment if demand is elastic
Pure benefit with no cost
Productivity to fall
Efficient outcomes
Wasted talent and inefficiency
Higher productivity for all
Equal pay automatically

mcqs.q: What does standard theory predict about a minimum wage?
options: A minimum wage always reduces unemployment because workers have more money to spend.
If above equilibrium, it raises wages for those still employed but causes unemployment by reducing labour demand — though empirical evidence is mixed.
GDP is income and GNP is spending.
A minimum wage is paid by the government.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between GDP and GNP?
options: GDP and GNP are the same thing with different names.
GDP measures output produced within a country's borders; GNP measures output produced by a country's nationals wherever they are.
PED measures whether a product is expensive or cheap.
GDP is income and GNP is spending.
